label: Circles and Cycles
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 443 through 464 and asks one question: when distance is induced by a Cayley-Klein absolute rather than primitive, what should count as a circle? The answer reframes every circle as a conic tied to the fundamental conic, and widens the word circle into the more flexible word cycle.

label: Distance Circles Are Conics
notes: Fix a center and collect all points at a fixed distance from it. Because the Cayley-Klein distance condition is quadratic in the moving point, the locus is automatically a conic, not a hand-drawn round shape. We never start from a Euclidean circle; we build the conic matrix directly from the absolute.

label: The Circle Pencil
notes: Every distance circle with center m lives in the pencil spanned by the skew zero-radius matrix M-transpose B M and the primal absolute A. Sliding the parameter sweeps from radius zero, a degenerate tangent pair through m, up to the absolute itself as the infinite-radius member. One formula generates the whole family.

label: Touching the Absolute
notes: All circles sharing a center meet the absolute at the same two exceptional points, where the polar of the center cuts the fundamental conic. There the tangent of the circle and the tangent of the absolute are proportional line vectors. In the Euclidean case those contacts are the two complex circular points every circle passes through.

label: Coaxial Pencils and Orthogonality
notes: Two circles are orthogonal exactly when each is apolar to the other through the absolute, a symmetric bilinear pairing of their matrices. Coaxial pencils and their orthogonal partners are conjugate families: one shares a radical structure, the other crosses every member at right angles, all expressed through the same fundamental conic.

label: Centers at Infinity
notes: Push the homogeneous center toward the line at infinity by letting its last coordinate vanish. Keeping one finite point fixed, the circle flattens: its finite trace becomes a straight line, and the missing component is the line at infinity. Projectively a line is just a circle whose center ran off to the horizon.

label: Circle, Horocycle, Hypercycle
notes: In hyperbolic geometry the center's position relative to the absolute classifies the cycle. An interior center gives an ordinary circle with no real boundary contact, a center on the absolute gives a horocycle with one real contact of higher multiplicity, and an exterior center gives a hypercycle meeting the boundary twice.

label: Dual Cycles and Contact
notes: Cycles also have a dual life: a center together with a signed parameter defines a primal conic and a dual conic that multiply to a scalar matrix. This Laguerre-flavored oriented-contact picture is why pencils, tangency, and inversion all behave coherently, and why the cross-ratio of four members stays invariant under projective change of chart.

label: Galilean Circles vs Cycles
notes: Galilean geometry is the warning case. Its distance reads only the x-coordinate difference, so a finite-distance circle collapses to a pair of vertical lines. That is far too small to carry a circle theory. The robust cycle objects are instead vertical parabolas, with the line pairs surviving as special degenerate members.

label: Galilean Cycle Theorems
notes: Familiar circle theorems survive on the standard cycle y equals x squared. The chord slope from parameter a to x simplifies to a plus x, so the peripheral angle becomes a slope difference independent of the viewpoint. The power of a point reappears as a secant product that depends only on the point, both checked symbolically.

label: Deforming Through Three Points
notes: Hold three finite points fixed and vary the ideal quadratic part x squared plus k y squared. Negative k gives two real ideal directions, positive k makes them complex, and k equal to zero coalesces them into the Galilean point at infinity. That middle conic is the vertical parabola, the cycle sitting exactly between hyperbola and ellipse.

label: Takeaways
notes: Carry away four ideas: a Cayley-Klein circle is a conic because constant distance is quadratic; the absolute fixes the shared contact points; a center at infinity yields a line plus the ideal line; and cycle bundles distance circles, limit conics, and dual curves that agree generically but split in degenerate geometries like the Galilean plane.
